Holiday Pay: How It Works, Typical Rates, and Your Rights

Direct AnswerHoliday pay explained: federal law does not require it, but most employers offer time-and-a-half or a paid day off. See rates, rules, and worked examples.

Gross pay estimates

Quick Answer

No federal law requires holiday pay in the United States — most employers offer it voluntarily, usually as time-and-a-half or a paid day off.

Here is the surprise at the heart of holiday pay in the United States: no federal law requires it. Not the paid day off, not time-and-a-half on Christmas, not double time on Thanksgiving. Yet most workers get some form of it — because employers offer it voluntarily. With Thanksgiving (Thursday, November 26, 2026) and Christmas (Friday, December 25, 2026) coming up, this guide explains exactly how holiday pay works, what the typical rates are, and how to calculate what a holiday shift is worth to you.

As the technical tools architect at Hourly Wage Converter, I build the calculators workers use to check premiums like these every day. The questions readers send us about holiday pay almost always start with a wrong assumption about the law — so this guide starts with the law, then gets practical: the three forms holiday pay takes, the 2026–2027 holiday calendar with verified dates, worked calculations at real pay rates, and what to do if your employer offers nothing at all.

The Short Answer: Holiday Pay in 60 Seconds

  • Not required by law: the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) does not require private employers to pay for holidays you take off, or to pay any premium for holidays you work.
  • Still very common: about 81% of private-sector workers receive paid holidays as a benefit, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics — it is a policy, not a right.
  • Typical premium: when employers pay extra for working a holiday, it is usually time-and-a-half (1.5×) or double time (2×) your regular rate.
  • Overtime is separate: the only premium federal law guarantees is 1.5× for hours you actually work beyond 40 in a workweek — and paid time off does not count toward those 40 hours.
  • The big 2026 dates: Thanksgiving is Thursday, November 26, and Christmas Day is Friday, December 25. Christmas Eve is not a federal holiday.
  • The exceptions: federal employees get holiday premium by statute, and a few state rules (Rhode Island is the best known) require premium pay for holiday work in some jobs.

Is Holiday Pay Mandatory? What the Law Actually Says

The Fair Labor Standards Act is the federal law that sets the minimum wage, overtime, and most pay rules for American workers — and it says nothing about holidays. The U.S. Department of Labor puts it plainly: the FLSA "does not require payment for time not worked, such as vacations or holidays," and holiday pay is generally a matter of agreement between an employer and an employee.

That one sentence produces three consequences that surprise people every November and December:

  • Your employer can schedule you on any holiday — Thanksgiving, Christmas, the Fourth of July — at your regular rate, as long as your total worked hours and pay stay within the normal minimum-wage and overtime rules.
  • If your employer closes for a holiday, federal law does not require them to pay hourly workers for that day. The paycheck simply shrinks unless a policy, contract, or salary arrangement says otherwise.
  • Time-and-a-half on a holiday is a gift or a bargain, not a statute. If your employer pays it, the obligation comes from their own handbook, your offer letter, or a union contract — which also means the details (which holidays, which roles, how much) are whatever that document says.

Two groups sit outside this rule. Federal government employees receive paid holidays and premium pay for holiday work under federal statute. Workers on certain federal contracts (under the Service Contract Act or Davis-Bacon Act) can have holiday terms written into their contract's wage determination. And at the state level, mandates are rare but real: Rhode Island, for example, requires most employers to pay time-and-a-half for work on Sundays and holidays. Everywhere else, assume the handbook rules — and read it.

How Holiday Pay Works: The Three Forms

When people say "holiday pay," they usually mean one of three different things. Knowing which one your employer offers matters, because they pay out very differently.

1. Paid time off on the holiday

The most common form: the business closes (or your department does), you stay home, and you are paid your normal wages for the day as if you had worked. For an hourly worker at $20 an hour on an 8-hour schedule, one paid holiday is worth $160 without working a minute. Salaried employees experience this as a salary that simply continues.

2. A premium rate for working the holiday

If the business stays open and you work, many employers pay a premium on top of — or instead of — the day off. The standard multipliers are time-and-a-half (1.5×) and double time (2×). Some employers pay the premium on top of a paid day off in the bank; most pay one or the other. Your policy document decides, which is why two people doing the same job at different companies can earn $160 or $320 for the same Christmas shift.

3. A floating holiday

Some employers give one or more "floating holidays" — paid days you can take on a day of your choosing — instead of, or in addition to, fixed company holidays. These are common where the workforce has diverse observances, and they are the usual answer when a fixed holiday falls on your scheduled day off.

How holiday pay interacts with overtime

This is where paychecks get confusing, so keep one rule in front of you: only hours you actually work count toward the 40-hour overtime threshold. Suppose Christmas week you work Monday to Thursday (32 hours), take Friday — Christmas Day — as a paid holiday (8 hours), and your paycheck shows 40 hours. You have earned no overtime, because only 32 of those hours were worked. Now suppose instead you work the Friday holiday too: 40 worked hours. Work Saturday as well and you reach 48 worked hours, so 8 hours must be paid at 1.5× under the FLSA — regardless of any holiday premium. Note that an employer can generally credit a voluntary holiday premium toward overtime it owes, so premium and overtime do not always stack. For the full mechanics, see our step-by-step overtime pay guide and our explainer on the 2026 overtime tax deduction.

Upcoming Holidays: Late 2026 and the 2027 Federal Calendar

There are 11 federal holidays. Private employers are not required to observe any of them — but most company holiday schedules are built from this list, so it is the calendar your own policy most likely follows. Dates and weekdays below are verified for 2026 and 2027.

Holiday Date Federal holiday?
Veterans DayWednesday, November 11, 2026Yes
Thanksgiving DayThursday, November 26, 2026Yes
Day after ThanksgivingFriday, November 27, 2026No — many employers close anyway
Christmas EveThursday, December 24, 2026No
Christmas DayFriday, December 25, 2026Yes
New Year's DayFriday, January 1, 2027Yes

The full 2027 federal list: New Year's Day (Friday, January 1), Martin Luther King Jr. Day (Monday, January 18), Presidents Day (Monday, February 15), Memorial Day (Monday, May 31), Juneteenth (Saturday, June 19 — observed Friday, June 18), Independence Day (Sunday, July 4 — observed Monday, July 5), Labor Day (Monday, September 6), Columbus Day (Monday, October 11), Veterans Day (Thursday, November 11), Thanksgiving (Thursday, November 25), and Christmas Day (Saturday, December 25 — observed Friday, December 24). "Observed" dates are when federal offices close when the holiday falls on a weekend; many private employers mirror them.

How to Calculate Holiday Pay (Worked Examples)

The math is simple once you know your multiplier. The formula is:

Holiday pay = hourly rate × multiplier × holiday hours worked (for a premium), or hourly rate × scheduled hours (for a paid day off).

Example 1: Time-and-a-half on Thanksgiving

You earn $18 an hour and work an 8-hour Thanksgiving shift at time-and-a-half. Your premium rate is $18 × 1.5 = $27 an hour, so the shift pays $27 × 8 = $216. The same shift at your regular rate would pay $144 — the holiday premium adds $72 to your day. (Our guide to whether premium pay is taxed at a higher rate explains why the bigger check can look over-taxed, and why it evens out at filing time.)

Example 2: Double time on Christmas

You earn $25 an hour, and your employer pays double time for Christmas Day. An 8-hour shift pays $25 × 2 × 8 = $400, versus $200 on a normal day. If your employer instead gives you the day off paid, the day is worth $200 without working.

Example 3: What a paid holiday is worth on salary

Salaried workers rarely see holiday pay as a line item, but it has a clear value. On a $62,400 salary, the standard daily rate is $62,400 ÷ 260 workdays (52 weeks × 5 days) = $240 a day. Eleven paid holidays a year are therefore worth about $2,640 of your compensation — worth remembering when you compare job offers with different holiday schedules.

Example 4: Part-time proration

You work 24 hours a week at $16 an hour, and your employer prorates holiday pay to your schedule. Your share is 24 ÷ 40 = 60%, so an 8-hour holiday pays 4.8 hours: 4.8 × $16 = $76.80. Not every employer prorates — some pay part-timers the full day, some pay nothing — but proration is the most common middle ground.

Who Gets Holiday Pay — and Who Usually Does Not

  • Salaried full-time employees: the most likely to receive the full package — paid holidays off, and often a premium or a substitute day if they must work one.
  • Hourly full-time employees: usually receive paid holidays after any probation period in the handbook; retail, healthcare, hospitality, and logistics commonly add 1.5× or 2× for working them, because the business must be staffed.
  • Part-time employees: the most variable group — prorated pay is common, full pay happens, and no pay is legal. The handbook decides.
  • Temporary, seasonal, and gig workers: usually no holiday pay at all. Independent contractors are outside employee benefit policies entirely (and outside the FLSA's employee protections).
  • Federal employees and many union members: holiday terms are set by statute or by the collective bargaining agreement — typically the most generous and the most precisely defined.

One practical note: many employers require you to work your scheduled shift before and after a holiday to qualify for the paid day — a rule aimed at unexcused long weekends. It is legal, it is common, and it is exactly the kind of detail buried in the handbook page nobody reads until December.

If Your Employer Does Not Offer Holiday Pay

Start by confirming it. Holiday terms hide in three places: the employee handbook, your offer letter or contract, and any union agreement. If a document promises a premium or a paid day and your paycheck does not show it, that is a broken promise you can enforce — show payroll the document and ask for a correction in writing.

If the policy genuinely offers nothing, you still have a few levers. Ask whether a floating holiday or shift swap is possible — managers grant these far more often than they grant cash. If you are comparing job offers, price the holiday schedule into the comparison: eleven paid holidays are worth roughly 4% of a salary, which can quietly beat a slightly higher offer with none. Finally, check your state labor department: a few states have premium-pay or reporting rules for specific industries, and state law can give you rights federal law does not.

One hard truth to close with: in most states, refusing a scheduled holiday shift carries no special federal protection — it is treated like refusing any shift. If you cannot work a holiday, raise it early and in writing; a swap arranged in October is a request, while the same ask on December 23rd is a problem.

Frequently Asked Questions About Holiday Pay

Answers to the six questions readers ask most are collected here; each also appears in the page’s structured data.

Is holiday pay mandatory in the US?

No. No federal law requires private employers to pay holiday pay. The Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) treats holidays like ordinary workdays: your employer does not have to give you the day off, pay you for a day you do not work, or pay a premium for working one. Whether you get holiday pay depends on your employer’s policy, your employment contract, or a union agreement. Federal government employees are the main exception, and a few state rules — Rhode Island is the best known — require premium pay for holiday work in some jobs.

How much is time and a half on $18 an hour?

Time and a half on $18 an hour is $27 an hour: $18 × 1.5 = $27. An 8-hour holiday shift at that rate pays $216, versus $144 at your regular rate — a $72 premium for the day. You can run your own rate and hours through our overtime calculator to get your exact number.

Do part-time employees get holiday pay?

Not by law — nothing in federal law guarantees holiday pay to part-time or full-time staff. Many employers do offer it to part-time workers on a prorated basis. A common formula pays the share of the holiday that matches your schedule: if you work 24 hours a week (60% of a 40-hour schedule), you might receive 60% of the full-time benefit — 4.8 hours of holiday pay instead of 8. Your employee handbook is where the actual rule lives.

What if a holiday falls on my day off?

Federal law gives you no right to a substitute day or extra pay when a holiday lands on your scheduled day off. Many employers voluntarily offer an alternate day off (sometimes called a floating holiday) in that situation, especially for salaried staff, but it is a policy choice, not a legal requirement. Check your handbook or ask HR before the holiday, not after.

Is Christmas Eve a paid holiday?

Christmas Eve — Thursday, December 24 in 2026 — is not a federal holiday, so there is no general right to pay for it. Some employers close early, give the full day, or treat it as a bonus holiday; others run a normal schedule. Christmas Day itself (Friday, December 25, 2026) is a federal holiday, though even then, private employers are not required by federal law to close or pay a premium.

Does holiday pay count toward overtime?

Only hours you actually work count toward the 40-hour overtime threshold. Paid holiday hours you took off do not count. If you work on the holiday, those hours count like any others — and once your worked hours pass 40 in a workweek, overtime at 1.5× your regular rate applies to every hour over 40. A holiday premium your employer pays voluntarily may be credited toward overtime they owe, so the two do not always stack on top of each other.

Key Takeaways & Action Plan

  • No law guarantees it: federal law does not require holiday pay — for most workers, the employee handbook is the law that matters. Read yours before the holidays, not after.
  • Know your multiplier: 1.5× and 2× are policy choices, and only hours you actually work count toward overtime’s 40-hour line.
  • Do the math before you volunteer: an 8-hour shift at $18 an hour and time-and-a-half pays $216 — run your own rate in the overtime calculator.
  • Mark the calendar: Thanksgiving is Thursday, November 26, 2026 and Christmas Day is Friday, December 25 — while Christmas Eve is not a federal holiday at all.
  • No premium? Check twice: look in your contract and your state’s rules, and ask about floating holidays — the answer is often better than the default.

Calculation Methodology & Sources

The legal summary reflects U.S. Department of Labor guidance on the Fair Labor Standards Act (holiday pay "is generally a matter of agreement between an employer and an employee"; the FLSA does not require payment for time not worked). The 81% figure is the Bureau of Labor Statistics estimate of private-industry workers with paid holidays. Holiday dates and weekdays were verified against the federal holiday schedule for 2026–2027, including weekend "observed" dates. Worked examples use the standard formulas in the calculation section; the salaried daily rate divides annual salary by 260 workdays (52 × 5). This article is general education, not legal or tax advice — your handbook, contract, and state rules control your actual pay. To model a paycheck with holiday hours, use our Paycheck Calculator or browse the Calculator Directory.

3 Things to Remember

  1. The FLSA does not require private employers to pay for holidays off or at a premium.
  2. It is still very common — about 81% of private-sector workers receive paid holidays, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
  3. When employers do pay extra for working a holiday, it is usually time-and-a-half (1.5×) or double time (2×) — and the 2026 dates are Thanksgiving, November 26, and Christmas, December 25.

Methodology & Data Verification

  • Basis: Pay figures are gross unless a section states take-home; tax figures use 2026 federal rules where shown.
  • Method: Full formulas, baselines, and rounding rules are on our calculation methodology page.
  • Coverage: U.S. federal rules; state and local rules vary and are not included.
  • Review: Last updated October 23, 2026.
  • Disclaimer: Estimates for planning only — not tax or legal advice.
